name: Febrile Urinary Tract Infection in Children
aliases: upper urinary tract infection in children

clinicalPearls: Fever with a urinary tract infection in a young child usually indicates upper tract involvement (pyelonephritis) and should be taken seriously because of the risk of renal scarring.
In infants and preverbal children, features are non-specific, so urinary tract infection must be considered in any young child with unexplained fever.
A properly collected urine specimen is essential; contamination from bag or non-clean-catch samples is a frequent source of misleading results.
Diagnosis rests on the combination of pyuria and a significant growth of a single uropathogen on culture from an appropriately obtained specimen.
Escherichia coli is the predominant pathogen, and prompt appropriate antibiotic treatment reduces the likelihood of renal injury.
Imaging, typically renal and bladder ultrasound, is used to detect structural abnormalities, with further studies such as voiding cystourethrography reserved for selected children.
Vesicoureteral reflux and other urinary tract abnormalities predispose to recurrent infection and scarring and should be considered, especially after atypical or recurrent infections.
Recurrent febrile infections and any resulting renal scarring can contribute to later hypertension and reduced renal function, so follow-up matters.
reference.pathophysiology: Most urinary tract infections are ascending: bowel-derived uropathogens, chiefly Escherichia coli, colonise the perineum, ascend the urethra, and multiply in the bladder. When bacteria and inflammation reach the kidney, pyelonephritis develops with fever and systemic signs. Bacterial virulence factors and host factors, including urinary stasis, incomplete bladder emptying, and vesicoureteral reflux that carries infected urine toward the kidney, promote upper tract infection. The inflammatory response within the renal parenchyma can injure tissue and, particularly with delayed treatment or recurrent episodes, lead to permanent scarring.
additionalDifferentials: Other sources of occult fever (e.g., bacteraemia, pneumonia)
Viral illness with incidental contaminated urine sample
Contaminated specimen giving a false-positive culture
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis or dipstick (leucocyte esterase, nitrites) and microscopy for pyuria
Urine culture from an appropriately collected specimen
Inflammatory markers and blood culture when systemically unwell
Voiding cystourethrography or renal scintigraphy in selected or recurrent cases
redFlags: Toxic appearance, signs of sepsis, or haemodynamic instability
Inability to tolerate oral fluids or oral antibiotics
Failure to improve on appropriate treatment
Known or suspected urinary tract abnormality or recurrent febrile infections
reference.prognosis: Most children with a promptly treated first febrile urinary tract infection recover fully, but recurrent infections, significant vesicoureteral reflux, or renal scarring carry a risk of long-term complications including hypertension and impaired renal function.
pitfalls: Diagnosing infection from a contaminated bag specimen instead of a properly collected sample
Failing to consider urinary tract infection in an infant with unexplained fever
Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria as if it were true infection
Neglecting follow-up imaging or evaluation after atypical or recurrent febrile infections
management: Start prompt empirical antibiotics targeting Escherichia coli and common uropathogens, guided by local resistance patterns and narrowed once urine culture sensitivities return
Use parenteral antibiotics for infants and children who are systemically unwell, vomiting or unable to tolerate oral therapy, switching to oral once clinically improving
Ensure adequate hydration and give antipyretics and analgesia such as paracetamol for fever and discomfort
Arrange renal and bladder ultrasound to detect structural abnormality, obstruction or hydronephrosis
Reserve voiding cystourethrography or DMSA scintigraphy for atypical, recurrent infection or abnormal ultrasound to assess vesicoureteral reflux and scarring
Consider antibiotic prophylaxis and refer to paediatric nephrology or urology for significant reflux, recurrent infection or established renal scarring
Institute long-term blood pressure and renal function surveillance where scarring is confirmed, and give clear safety-net advice to re-present urgently with recurrent fever or deterioration
